title: Four Moves for US Companies in a New Cost Environment
gist: BCG argues that a K-shaped consumer economy, tariffs and supply chain risk, organizational complexity, activism and AI have made incremental US cost programs obsolete, and that structural cost resets are followed by EV/EBIT multiple expansion. It prescribes four moves: a C-suite structural reset, reinvest by segment, board-level zero-based governance, and AI-enabled diagnostics.

themes.theme: Five forces behind the cost reset

insights.claim: BCG argues five converging forces (K-shaped consumer economy, geopolitical volatility, elevated labor cost/complexity, shareholder activism, AI) make conventional incremental cost programs obsolete for US companies.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Frame for screening which companies are still running legacy cost programs and are exposed to forced, reactive cuts.
insights.locator: Converging Forces Demand a Structural Reset

insights.claim: Consumer discretionary companies that entered 2023 with higher margins have outperformed lower-margin peers on margin expansion, TSR and revenue growth, because stronger margins let them absorb pressure in value segments while investing in premium.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Margin starting point is a factor in discretionary winners; favor high-margin names in a bifurcated consumer.
insights.locator: The K-shaped economy necessitates dual-speed performance

insights.claim: Fading pandemic-era support for lower-income households, alongside rising asset values for higher-income households, has split the US consumer market since 2023, yet most companies run a single cost system built for one consumer type.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Companies with a single cost model serving both ends are mismatched; watch for value/premium split in results.
insights.locator: The K-shaped economy necessitates dual-speed performance

insights.claim: Competing in a K-shaped economy requires a dual cost structure: radical efficiency to serve value-oriented customers and sustained investment to capture premium demand.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Look for firms explicitly segmenting cost bases by customer tier.
insights.locator: Competing effectively in this bifurcated economy

insights.claim: Supply chain disruption risk has risen sharply versus the previous decade and recovery periods now average more than eight months, making efficiency-optimized static cost models fragile.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Efficiency-only supply chains carry underpriced tail risk; resilience costs will weigh on margins.
insights.locator: Geopolitical volatility has made static cost models obsolete

insights.claim: The average effective US tariff rate rose to about 17% by April 2025 from 2.2% at end-2024; a 2026 Supreme Court ruling curtailed many tariffs but policy remains in flux.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Tariff policy remains a live cost and margin risk factor to monitor.
insights.locator: Tariffs have added another layer of complexity

insights.claim: Resilience measures such as supplier diversification, footprint changes and inventory buffers are right but costly, and legacy complexity like sprawling supplier networks and redundant processes can masquerade as resilience without reducing risk.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Distinguish real resilience spend from legacy complexity when judging cost bases.
insights.locator: The common strategic responses to this environment

insights.claim: High labor costs are often rooted in accumulated organizational complexity (layers, duplicated functions, blurred decision rights from growth, M&A and digital investment) that annual head count reviews rarely surface; across-the-board cuts may remove capabilities without fixing it.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Serial acquirers carry hidden structural cost; blunt layoffs may hurt capability without lasting margin gain.
insights.locator: Labor costs remain elevated, but complexity is the deeper problem

themes.theme: Activism and AI as pressure points

insights.claim: Activists now demand structural margin resets, portfolio simplification and operating model redesign rather than overhead trims, and cost management has become a board-level governance issue alongside capital allocation.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Companies that have not elevated cost to board level are prime activist targets.
insights.locator: Shareholder activism has returned, with sharper demands

insights.claim: Investors now expect AI to show margin impact rather than pilots, but AI cannot generate reliable insight where cost data is fragmented, siloed or ownership is ambiguous.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: AI productivity claims are credible only where cost data foundations are strong; probe for that in earnings narratives.
insights.quote: The window for AI experimentation is closing. Investors expect to see margin impact, not pilots.

insights.claim: Among US companies that completed cost resets from 2016 through 2026, most saw meaningful expansion in three-year average forward EV/EBIT multiples after the reset, as investors read it as a signal of management execution capacity.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Structural cost resets are a possible re-rating catalyst; screen for announced resets.
insights.locator: Cost Resets Move Valuations—Not Just Margins

insights.claim: Investors appear to distinguish between programs that merely trim costs and structural transformations that rethink capital allocation and operating model, making cost architecture a valuation issue.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Re-rating depends on reset depth, not just savings size.
insights.locator: Cost Resets Move Valuations—Not Just Margins

insights.claim: Companies deferring a structural reset accumulate risk: a widening valuation discount as the performance gap grows, more exposure to activists, and less capacity to absorb the next macro shock.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Laggards are candidates for discounts and activist campaigns.
insights.locator: Investors are rewarding companies with cost architectures

themes.theme: Four imperatives for the new cost agenda

insights.claim: A structural reset means redesigning the organization as if built from scratch for the future portfolio, confronting accumulated complexity and choosing explicitly where to be leaner than competitors versus invest more, owned by the C-suite and board.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Reset depth and executive ownership are the signals to look for in management commentary.

insights.claim: Common tools such as head count targets, SG&A reviews and procurement savings address symptoms of a misaligned cost base without touching the architecture that produced it.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Announced traditional programs are unlikely to deliver durable margin change.
insights.quote: They address the symptoms of a misaligned cost base without touching the architecture that produced the misalignment.

insights.claim: Reinvestment logic differs by segment: savings in price-sensitive segments should strengthen unit economics and price competitiveness, while in premium segments they should fund capabilities and experiences that defend margin.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Check whether savings are directed to segment-appropriate reinvestment rather than absorbed into margin.
insights.locator: 2. Reset costs across the business, then reinvest with discipline

insights.claim: Most organizations struggle with cost not for lack of ambition but for lack of governance to make tradeoffs explicit, so savings are deployed too broadly or absorbed into margin while higher-return uses stay underfunded.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Weak governance explains why savings fail to convert into growth investment.
insights.locator: 2. Reset costs across the business, then reinvest with discipline

insights.claim: Zero-based principles should sit under board oversight of capital allocation, not just the CFO budget process, so that they are sustained rather than episodic and fund growth rather than starve it.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Board-level zero-based discipline signals a durable reset.

insights.claim: AI-enabled diagnostics can isolate cost drivers, surface duplication and detect margin leakage in real time, turning cost management from an annual review into a continuous discipline; AI amplifies rather than replaces structural cost discipline.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: AI cost tooling is an enabler for firms with governance already in place.
insights.locator: 4. Use AI to accelerate the reset and sustain the gains
